newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Melbourne airport buyers see cargo opportunities.
newsitem.headline: Melbourne airport buyers see cargo opportunities.

text.p: The winning consortium for Melbourne's international airport said on Wednesday a priority for the group was to study opportunities for developing property at the airport, in particular cargo sheds.
"We will be looking at property development potential in the short to medium term," Andrew Jurenko, the chief executive of Asia Pacific Airports (APA) told reporters at a media briefing.
"We would like to get to know quickly the people who move live produce into Asia to see whether or not they are happy with the facilities on the ground," he said.
"I think we will have a far more productive approach to property (than the Federal Airports Corp) - the key thing will be that it will be aviation related."

The APA consortium comprises British airport operator, BAA Plc with an initial 25.1 percent stake, insurance and funds group Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP) with 49.9 percent and Sydney-based funds manager Axiom with 25 percent.
BAA's stake would fall to 15.1 percent if a proposed fourth partner, Melbourne-based Hastings Funds Management, exercised its option to take a 10 percent stake.
Axiom was last week sold to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell by the New South Wales government for A$240 million.
The Australian government said earlier that APA would pay A$1.307 billion for Melbourne Airport.

The consortium partners would introduce total equity of A$350 million, Jurenko said, with A$850 million of senior debt from Westpac Banking Corp and Britain's National Westminister Bank and the remainder being funded by AMP.
Jurenko, formerly the managing director of BAA Pacific Ltd, said APA had forecast an internal rate of return for the airport of between 13.8 percent to 14 percent over a ten year period.
"AMP and Axiom are long-term investors. We want to ensure the airport is well run and get it stabilised before we think about that and that is some years away," Threadgold said.
Jurenko added that BAA was also a long term investor.
He said the consortium had valued the airport on the basis of cashflow, not by earnings multiple.
Jurenko said BAA would not manage the airport with most of the expertise coming from consultants.
"APA needs those services in order to demonstate that it is the (airport's) operator," he said.
AMP's representative in the consortium, chief general manager Andrew Threadgold, told reporters the consortium had no immediate plans to float.
